blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The concept of biodiversity hotspots was introduced by Norman Myers in 1988 to designate regions featuring exceptional levels of plant endemism under high degree of threat.

To qualify as a biodiversity hotspot, a region must contain at least 1,500 species of endemic vascular plants (>0.5% of world total) and must have lost at least 70% of its original primary vegetation.
India is home to 4 globally recognized biodiversity hotspots: The Himalayas, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma region, and Sundaland (which includes the Nicobar group of islands).
Biodiversity hotspots cover only about 2.5% of the Earth's land surface, yet they support more than half of the world's plant species as endemics.
Conservation International (CI) and the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF) play central roles in designating and funding biodiversity hotspots worldwide.

rows: Entire Indian Himalayan Region (Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh)
Snow Leopard, Himalayan Tahr, Musk Deer
Continuous chain along western coast through Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu
Lion-tailed Macaque, Nilgiri Tahr, Malabar Grey Hornbill
North-Eastern states (south of Brahmaputra), Andaman Islands
Sangai Deer, Hoolock Gibbon, Edible-nest Swiftlet
Nicobar Megapode, Crab-eating Macaque, Leatherback Turtle

items: Norman Myers coined the term 'Biodiversity Hotspot' in 1988; this scientist-year pairing is a frequent UPSC Prelims question.
Nicobar Islands are part of the Sundaland hotspot, whereas the Andaman Islands belong to the Indo-Burma hotspot.
Always distinguish between 'Hotspots' (Myers/CI) and 'Hope Spots' (Mission Blue/Ocean conservation) in Environment MCQs.
